quote:
Superhuman had the biggest head start on email. In 2018/2019 there was a waitlist to get personally onboarded and taught how to use email. People waited weeks and would brag about getting access.

7 years later, they completely missed the boat on integrating AI. They should be able to draft emails that sound like me - after all, they have tens of thousands of emails to reference.

IMO, the Grammarly acquisition is pairing two companies that missed a window where they had leverage (users, data, funding) to build a significant product.

Leading up to the acquisition, Superhuman was valued at $800m+ on (what I’ve heard) is like <$3m ARR.

The product stayed the same for years and the user base never really grew? Or it churned like crazy?

Not sure what to make of the redesign, but it feels like Superhuman is moving to a suite/ OS of work tools, when the remaining users….
just want it to be good at email.

Not calendars, not a personal assistant, just good at sending emails quickly.

Been trying Slashy over the last month.

It sends emails that actually sound like me.

Guess I’m switching.

He was playing basketball in loafers, which isn't the wisest decision he's ever made. He couldn't type for over a month. Fortunately, the email client he had built by hand could cover for him. "I was in immense pain, but I didn't miss a day of work," [he said](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/harsha-gaddipati-032bb820a_sprained-both-my-wrists-luckily-slashy-share-7424339442074697728-ZgFL/).

Slashy (not to be confused with Slash) is an AI-native email client based in San Francisco and backed by Y Combinator, where it went through the Summer 2025 batch. Ever since AI started scaling as quickly as it did in the early 2020's, email has been one of the most obvious places to put it. That's why so many have taken a run at it -- Gmail got Gemini a while back, Outlook got CoPilot, and Grammarly bought Superhuman.

However, Slashy goes far beyond the quick summaries, grammar fixes, and one-sentence reply suggestions of the more popular

quote:
I put a new company into our CRM this morning and never opened the CRM.

@slashyemail moved @attio lists into the email sidebar.

The thread was a cold pitch. A founder had emailed three times about his GTM tool, and this morning I answered: I'm happy with what I'm already running, both of them driven from the terminal, so a third tool to evaluate isn't where my week should go. If his does something specific that mine don't, I'll take the call.

That is the most common verdict in business and the one nobody writes down. Not now, but not never.

So I gave it somewhere to live. Company added to our Suppliers list, stage set to Evaluation, category Software/SaaS, and a one-line note on what the product actually is. All of it in the sidebar of the message I was answering.

That last part is what makes it useful. Not that lists are visible from the inbox, but that the list entry's own attributes are editable there. Membership on its own is a label. Stage, category and a note are a judgment.

You can also skip the fields and say it: "add the company to our Suppliers list".

What I keep coming back to is where records are born. Companies don't arrive through your CRM. They arrive through an email, a form, an intro, and the CRM is where they go afterwards. That gap between meeting a company and having it in the system is small, and it's exactly where the maybes fall out.

Close it and a maybe survives contact with the week.

The open question arrives with it. If records can be created and changed from the inbox, the inbox is now a place where records change. That's an ownership question, and I don't think it has a general answer yet. For two people it's obviously fine. At fifteen I'd want to know who can move what, and from where.

"Maybe later" is the most common answer anyone will give you, and the least recorded. Not because it doesn't matter. Because until now, writing it down cost more than it was worth.
